fixes.why: The note states the reading's own inference as if it were the verse's content: 'which sets believing and obeying side by side'. The Berean renders the word 'rejects', and holders of the faith-alone readings take the verse as the contrast of believing with unbelief. A note that stands only for reading 3 tilts the card toward it.
fixes.fix: Replace the note with: "Read as setting believing and obeying side by side: the Greek word the Berean renders “rejects” is glossed in MACULA as “not obeying”. Holders of the other readings take the same verse as the contrast between believing and unbelief."

fixes.why: The note defends the Catholic sense of the word ('it does not name earning apart from grace') in Catholic terms and leaves out the Reformation objection to the term. A Lutheran or Reformed reader would see the term softened on the Catholic side only.
fixes.fix: Replace the note with: "The Catholic term for the reward that God's grace makes due to works done in grace. Lutheran and Reformed writers reject the term, holding that no work of the believer makes a person's standing before God due."

fixes.where: Reading 2, passages: replace Romans 11:6 with Genesis 15:6
fixes.why: Romans 4:3 quotes Genesis 15:6, and reading 2 rests on that quotation, yet the Old Testament verse itself appears nowhere. The rabbi seat asks for the Hebrew Scripture in its own words, and the Lutheran and Reformed seats would expect the root text. Romans 11:6 is the weaker of reading 2's verses for its holders. The count stays at 8. The rule on the Old Testament is met because the note says the reading is theirs.
fixes.fix: Replace the Romans 11:6 passage with {"ref": "Genesis 15:6", "quote": "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.", "note": "The verse Romans 4:3 quotes. Lutheran and Reformed writers read it as the Old Testament account of trust credited as righteousness."}. Under the rabbi's seat the note should also state that this is the Christian reading of the verse, not the verse's own sense. The rabbi seat should confirm that wording.

fixes.why: The card reads Genesis 22 only through James 2:21-23 in reading 2's answers, and gives the Hebrew story no words of its own. The rabbi seat asks that the Old Testament speak in its own voice. The Catholic and Eastern Orthodox seats cite the offering of Isaac as an example of works.
fixes.fix: Append to the answers text: "Holders of this reading also point to Genesis 22:18, where the blessing of the nations comes “because you have obeyed My voice”, and read the offering of Isaac in that light."

fixes.where: Reading 1, passage Romans 2:6 replaced by James 2:15
fixes.why: James 2:14-17 is the passage in which the card's own topic is worked out in practice, and the card cites James 2:17, 2:22 and 2:24 but not the case James puts forward. Holders of the works reading, and readers attentive to justice in many Black and global churches, would expect it. Romans 2:6 says the same thing in general terms and is still cited in reading 2's answers, so the swap loses nothing. The count stays at 8.
fixes.fix: Replace the Romans 2:6 passage with {"ref": "James 2:15", "quote": "Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food.", "note": "Faith tested in practice: James 2:14-17 asks what good faith is when a brother or sister is in need."}.

fixes.why: 'who stand in the Wesleyan holiness line' places the Pentecostal and Charismatic movements inside the Wesleyan lineage and passes over their origin in African American and multiracial revival. A reader outside the white mainstream would see the card placing the white Wesleyan line at the centre.
fixes.fix: Replace the sentence "Pentecostal and Charismatic readers who stand in the Wesleyan holiness line share much of this, and others in those traditions hold the second reading." with "Pentecostal and Charismatic readers, many of whose movements grew out of the holiness revivals, including the Azusa Street revival led by African American preachers, share much of this, and others in those traditions hold the second reading."

fixes.why: 'which a believer is called to keep and can leave' compresses the Wesleyan view of falling away into a phrase that sounds like a casual aside. A Wesleyan reader would want the claim attributed as the tradition's own teaching.
fixes.fix: Replace "which a believer is called to keep and can leave" with "which a believer is called to keep, and from which, Wesleyan writers hold, a believer can fall away".

summary: Every card quote is the Berean's exact text, and the readings take no side, but the John 3:36 note and the merit term lean toward one reading, and the card leaves out Genesis 15:6, Genesis 22 and the James 2 case of need, which the rabbi and the young believer seats would notice. Seven fixes, each keeping eight passages per reading, would let every seat accept it.
